text: This is why we look to industry practitioners, who know how the market works and are in contact with the buyers and sellers, to make a judgement based on their experience while we provide guidance on what they should look out for.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Under the third prong of our anti-money laundering strategy, which is enforcement, our sectoral regulators play an important role in ensuring that gatekeepers carry out their responsibilities properly.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: CEA has made considerable effort to help property agents and agencies carry out their responsibilities.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: First, to educate the industry, CEA has issued a guide to property agents and agencies on compliance with anti-money laundering regulations.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It provides details on the checks to be conducted and the measures that need to be put in place, including checklists to guide agents and agencies in fulfilling their CDD obligations.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Second, CEA provides a list of common suspicious indicators to aid agents and agencies in identifying suspicious transactions.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: These include: buying multiple properties within a short time; purchasing properties without inspecting them; and entering into transactions at a value much higher or lower than market value.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Third, CEA regularly shares latest developments and responses to common queries by property agents and agencies relating to their anti-money laundering duties.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: CEA is also developing a one-stop resource webpage to make it easier for the industry to retrieve information on anti-money laundering requirements.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Fourth, property agents who require additional training on their anti-money laundering duties may take up the continuing professional development course provided by CEA's course providers.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Like CEA, the URA regularly conducts briefings and has been issuing circulars to guide developers in their duties, even before the legislation had been passed earlier this year.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: As part of ensuring compliance, CEA and URA conduct anti-money laundering-related inspections regularly.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Property agents, agencies, and developers that are identified to be of higher risk are prioritised for inspections and subject to more regular inspections.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For example, those who deal more in private housing, especially higher-end projects, could be considered higher risk.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: CEA and URA also conduct ad hoc inspections based on feedback from law enforcement agencies on possible infringements by property agents, agencies and developers.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We would also like to point out that besides the developers, property agencies and agents, professionals such as conveyancing lawyers, accountants and financial institutions, who similarly have anti-money laundering obligations, are also involved in nearly all property transactions.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: As highlighted by Minister Josephine, lawyers and accountants also have strict KYC and anti-money laundering obligations.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Conveyancing lawyers and the relevant accountants are required to perform CDD when preparing for or carrying out any acquisition, divestment or any other dealing of any interest in real estate.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: These professionals are also required to file an STR with the STRO if in the course of their business or profession, these professionals know or have reasonable grounds to suspect that any property may be connected to criminal conduct.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Apart from these legal obligations, lawyers and accountants who are mindful of their professional reputations and risk exposure would and should decline to act for the potential client in the suspicious transactions.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim asked whether there are differences between financial institutions and property agents in implementing anti-money laundering measures.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In general, while the underlying principles are the same, the anti-money laundering measures required must be tailored to address risks unique to the sector and the party involved.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Principally, as my colleagues have emphasised, our regime is a comprehensive one.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Any person who knows or has reasonable grounds to suspect that any property represents the proceeds of, or is connected with criminal conduct, is required to file an STR to the Police.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: To answer Mr Murali Pillai's question, this includes landlords, if they have reasonable grounds to suspect their tenants.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Failure to file such STRs as soon as reasonably practicable is an offence.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In sum, in the real estate sector, there are several layers of defence to mitigate risks of money-laundering and protect the system from abuse.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The gatekeepers cover different areas, but play complementary roles in strengthening prevention and detection in our regime.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: As such, the vast majority of purchase and sale transactions are subject to CDD checks, in some form and at various stages.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In fact, most of them are subject to more than one layer of checks.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: If any of the gatekeepers fall short of their duties or do not carry out their obligations, they will be subject to penalties.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Enforcement is taken by CEA and URA, our sectoral regulators who also work hard to guide our gatekeepers in their responsibilities.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Next, let me address Members' questions on the Government's efforts to detect illicit activities conducted by or through companies incorporated in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Our regulatory regime seeks to balance between maintaining the ease of doing business, which has been the hallmark of Singapore as a business and financial hub and ensuring strong corporate governance to uphold investors' confidence.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Today, the Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority (ACRA) has in place various measures to deter the misuse of companies for money laundering.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In response to Members' questions, let me first describe the baseline framework that ACRA has in place, before I explain the additional measures that are in place for intermediaries such as Registered Filing Agents, which similarly follow the spirit of prevention, detection and enforcement.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: As and when there are changes to the directorships, companies will need to update ACRA accordingly and the new additions will be screened.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This goes beyond the requirements of many other jurisdictions.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Non-resident foreigners looking to set up companies in Singapore will therefore need to either appoint a resident business partner as a director, or appoint a nominee director to act on their behalf.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Post-incorporation, ACRA monitors companies and takes proactive enforcement measures to guard against their potential misuse.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked about the prevalence of non-trading or inactive companies and how ACRA addresses the issue.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: There are various reasons why an owner may choose to keep his company despite not actively operating it, for example, due to other business priorities, illness or other challenges.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: A clear sign of inactivity is when a company fails to file its annual returns.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: As companies could be inactive due to legitimate reasons, ACRA does not take action immediately.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Instead, ACRA continues to track such companies and if they remain inactive after a period, or are flagged via intelligence provided by other agencies, ACRA will proceed to strike them off.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Thus far, the companies associated with this case have largely been filing annual returns with ACRA and have thus remained on the register.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I should clarify, however, that not all companies that are being misused for money laundering are inactive or dormant firms.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Criminals often use front companies with a portfolio of businesses, comprising a mix of legitimate and illicit activities.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This makes it challenging for regulators to identify the true nature of companies, unless active investigations of the company's activities are undertaken.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The checks that I have mentioned apply to all companies in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The first relates to the role that Registered Filing Agents play in mitigating the risks posed by foreign-owned companies.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: As a business hub, we attract many foreign companies to Singapore.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: By and large, they are bona fide, and we welcome them because they contribute to our economy and provide good jobs for our locals.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: However, we recognise that there could be some bad actors, who may take advantage of Singapore's pro-business environment and open financial markets to conduct illicit activities.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, as part of our prevention efforts, we therefore impose additional requirements on foreign-owned or foreign-controlled companies.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Non-residents who are looking to set up companies in Singapore must engage ACRA-authorised corporate service providers, also known as Registered Filing Agents, to incorporate a company.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Registered Filing Agents provide another layer of scrutiny, which is particularly useful for foreign-owned or controlled companies, in addition to ACRA's pre-incorporation checks.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Registered Filing Agents are legally required to: one, conduct CDD, by identifying and verifying the identities of the customer and the beneficial owners of the intended incorporated company; two, conduct enhanced CDD to compensate for the higher risk if the customer is not physically present, such as ensuring that the customer's identity is established by additional documents or information, and three, inquire into the purpose and legitimacy of the use of a company structure.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: If the Registered Filing Agent fails to complete the due diligence measures, it must not proceed with the intended incorporation transaction and should file an STR.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Registered Filing Agents should also file STRs if they encounter any suspicious transactions in the course of their work.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This helps to alert authorities of risks surrounding specific companies.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Registered Filing Agents play an important role as gatekeepers in reducing the likelihood of a Singapore entity being incorporated and subsequently misused for money laundering.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: They are subject to supervision by ACRA for compliance with AML/CFT obligations.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: ACRA takes enforcement actions on Registered Filing Agents found to have breached any requirement.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: ACRA is investigating the role played by the Registered Filing Agents involved in this case, and will take enforcement action if necessary.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: [Please refer to "Clarification by Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development", Official Report, 3 October 2023, Vol 95, Issue 113, Correction By Written Statement section.] ACRA has planned additional measures, such as enhancing the penalties on errant service providers, to strengthen the effectiveness of our anti-money laundering regime.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Because of Singapore's requirement for companies to appoint at least one ordinarily resident director, foreigners based overseas often look for local nominee directors to act on their behalf on matters relating to their company.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: To address this need, corporate service providers provide services for nominee directors to be appointed, among other services.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: As some individuals take on nominee directorships as a business service, it is understandable for them to hold multiple directorships, to support their clients in due diligence checks and incorporating their business.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Nominee directors have the same legal obligations as other directors and are required to discharge their duties responsibly, with honesty and reasonable diligence.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Those who fail to do so can face sanctions, including disqualification and debarment.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Melvin Yong asked about the number of individuals who have held a large number of directorships.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In line with international benchmarks like the UK, US and Australia, there are currently no limits to the number of companies that a director can be involved in.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: ACRA has been studying restrictions on directorships, both to ensure that nominee directors are fit and proper to take up the role and whether it would be useful to limit the number of nominee directorships that one can hold.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: These proposals were put out for public consultation in 2022.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We will take into account risk factors and business needs, in deciding whether to introduce additional measures.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: These proposals will also be tabled in Parliament early next year.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: ACRA manages a central register of controllers, which sets out the beneficial owners of companies, that is, the individuals who ultimately own or control a company.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This data on beneficial ownership is crucial in combating money laundering and foiling the plans of criminals.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It aids law enforcement agencies in their investigations, by enabling them to peel back the different layers, identify the criminals behind the companies that are used for illicit activities and bring them to task.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: To maintain its data quality, ACRA conducts regular inspections to ensure that companies file their beneficial ownership information in a timely manner.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Enforcement action is taken on those who fail to comply.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: As part of its detection efforts, ACRA utilises data analytics to identify individuals who may be nominee directors of high-risk companies that are potentially being misused, as well as Registered Filing Agents who might be involved in the setup of such companies.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In addition, as Minister Teo mentioned earlier, as a sectoral regulator, ACRA works closely with STRO and law enforcement agencies, and flags high-risk individuals to them regularly for more in-depth review.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: ACRA also undertakes checks and takes action with the help of intelligence received from other agencies, such as the CAD.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Should ACRA or CAD's investigations uncover any wrongdoing, ACRA will take action to impose sanctions on the Registered Filing Agent, which could include cancellation or suspension, and against the company and its directors.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Notwithstanding all these efforts from various agencies, our anti-money laundering efforts are an unending endeavour.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: As this case has shown, criminals are becoming increasingly sophisticated.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Even as we identify new areas to tighten, criminals will inevitably find new loopholes to exploit.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: As criminals will constantly find new ways to circumvent our laws and regulations, Government agencies and relevant industry players must become ever more coordinated to successfully uncover and arrest money laundering.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: To this end, we must strengthen our information-gathering and intel-sharing capabilities so that we can better detect illicit activities conducted by companies incorporated in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: To ensure that our anti-money laundering regime remains robust, the inter-agency steering committee will continue to oversee the WOG anti-money laundering efforts.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Where gaps are identified, we will tighten our regulations and enforcement to prevent exploitation by criminals.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Committee will share its progress and findings in due time.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We will continue to uphold our zero-tolerance approach towards money laundering and do our best to ensure a strong and robust regulatory regime.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Should the queries be sufficiently addressed, it may not be necessary for Members to pose identical PQs for the future Sittings.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I know there is a lot of interest in this subject which is why 30 Members have filed a total of 57 PQs for the last Sitting and this Sitting.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I will make sure that everyone who have filed PQs will be given an opportunity to seek clarifications.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But before I call on Members for clarifications, I wish to point out two Standing Orders to guide Members and to facilitate discussions on the Ministerial Statements.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Members can seek clarifications by way of asking questions.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, I seek Members' understanding to keep your clarifications clear and concise so that Ministers can answer as many clarifications as possible.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Likewise, I would also ask the Ministers to also keep your answers clear and concise.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I will ask the Clerks to help me spot all the hands.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But I will call on Mr Murali Pillai first.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Practitioners in the area often refer to assets from ill-gotten gains as "oxygen" for the criminals.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I invite hon Members in this House to join me to congratulate the Police force for a job well-done.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Members may also access the handout through the MP@SGPARL app.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Whilst the materials are making their way to the Members, Mr Murali Pillai, in his question, referred to FATF and the mutual evaluations that are being conducted by FATF.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And FATF, as an international organisation that sets standards for the prevention of money laundering, is well-recognised for several things.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For one thing, the standards that FATF has set are adopted by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, as far as the IMF and the World Bank are concerned, FATF's standards are gold standards.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If you are a serious financial centre and you meet those standards, then, in a sense, you have passed the test.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But how does one get evaluated against the standards?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, what Mr Murali referred to are mutual evaluations.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These are experts that are drawn from within FATF itself as an organisation as well as a global network of expert practitioners.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, individuals like that are held in high regard.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But what was said after the evaluation in 2016?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I quote from the FATF report and it says, "Singapore has a strong legal and institutional framework to fight money laundering and terrorist financing.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Singapore's AML/CFT coordination is highly sophisticated and inclusive of all relevant competent authorities." It says that we are highly sophisticated and inclusive of all relevant competent authorities.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Murali's question is: how does it put us in comparison to other jurisdictions?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It puts us in good standing when compared to leading jurisdictions like Australia.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But because the evaluations are done at different times, it is not possible to treat this as an apple-for-apple comparison.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: What we do have, if you refer to the handout, under Annex A, I think there is a Table 1 which provides the ratings that Singapore was awarded in eight outcome areas that were relevant to money laundering.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We have also, in Table 1, reflected the ratings that were awarded to other leading jurisdictions who were evaluated around the same time as Singapore.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It does not mean after the evaluation, we sit still, we are happy with what we have gotten.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In all that seven years that have since passed, we have made significant progress in enhancing our anti-money laundering regime.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For example, we have strengthened the regime for non-financial sectors.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: What I talked about earlier, DNFBPs, that would fall under one category.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We have also enhanced the pursuit of cross-border money laundering offences and confiscation of proceeds of crime by all law enforcement agencies, including through international cooperation.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And this ongoing case is an excellent example of our efforts.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But apart from what FATF says, I would like to draw Members' attention to another index that is known as the Basel Anti-Money Laundering Index.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And the latest Index was tabulated in 2022.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I am afraid I have not been able to include it in the handout.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But there were 128 regions that were ranked in the Basel Anti-Money Laundering Index.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And if you are at 128, that is the lowest risk.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But lowest risk can also mean that nothing is happening in your region.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, you may not be a financial centre of any scale.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, I do not think it is possible for Singapore to aim to be number 128.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It would mean that we do not really have a financial centre of international importance.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This ranking puts us ahead of the US, Switzerland as well as financial hubs, such as Hong Kong and Dubai.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, I think the facts do speak for themselves.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Following up from where Second Minister for Finance had suggested, I would ask Members, for this first set of clarifications, if they could centre around clarifications on the anti-money laundering system.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, that is the first segment we will try to cover.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: And then, we will move to the financial system and sector.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: And then, we will move on to real estate.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: And then, we will move on to companies, immigration and work passes.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: And finally, the last one is an open category.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, for the first series of clarification, let us try to centre it around the anti-money laundering system.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: How is it that these monies could also be spent in various types of transactions?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I explained during my Statement that when we set up our strategies for prevention of money laundering, we must understand that it is not all about prevention only.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We must know from the outset that however stringent the measures we put in place, criminal actors, money launderers, will find ways and means to still take advantage of our openness and our solid reputation as a sound financial centre.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is precisely because of our openness and precisely because we are deemed to have a very high reputation that the money launderers find us just as attractive as the legitimate investors.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, we must know that they are resolved, they are determined to try and circumvent the rules that we have put in place.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Therefore, the strategy must also include detection and enforcement.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If we merely had prevention and then imagine that all is well and good, we are kidding no one else but ourselves.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And, so, it is useful for us to remember if we do not detect any cases at all and, more importantly, if we are not able to mount a robust response by way of enforcement and taking these criminals to task, it does not necessarily speak better of the robustness of our anti-money laundering regime.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In this particular instance, we have uncovered a very large web.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I do not mean to cast aspersions on other regimes.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But the examples that I cited shows you how difficult it is to round up criminals.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Some of the amounts that I cited, if we think that that is all there is to the illicit funds that are sloshing around in these other regimes, I think that is not being very realistic.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, the strength of our regime is also in detection and then, to be able to enforce in a decisive and robust manner.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We might have found a much smaller amount and we might have patted ourselves on the back and said, "That was not too bad.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Well done." But, in fact, we would have missed an opportunity to get to the root of the problem and to try our very best to stamp it out.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First, is MAS of the view that our existing penalties imposed on financial institutions for breaches of anti-money laundering measures are sufficiently deterrent and are the financial penalties linked to the amount that is being laundered?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Second, what sort of penalties have been imposed on the real estate companies or agents for breaching anti-money laundering measures?

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: As my colleagues have mentioned, there are three prongs to the approach towards anti-ML/TF.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The key to this is the first prong, which is prevention, and MAS regularly reviews all of our AML/CFT procedures.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We review them as we go along and, of course, regularly as well.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The first also is that, given that there are huge financial flows into the system – millions of transactions every day – the same qualities which are strengths in our financial system will also be exploited by criminals.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Although we need strict controls for our anti-money laundering regime, I think we need to balance that with the cost of due diligence and overburdening our businesses for checks and reporting.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What are the steps to sensemake and regularly consult the stakeholders, particularly financial institutions, pawnbrokers and our precious stone and metal dealers as well?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To Mr Zhulkarnain's question, in fact, our sectoral regulators engage with their gatekeepers very regularly.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Earlier this year, for example, because of the impending changes in our PSPM Act, MinLaw had engaged with the industry behind closed doors to get a sense of what they were observing and to also find out if the additional measures that MinLaw was intending, was thinking about, would be too onerous to implement and also, more importantly, to what extent they could be effective.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: MAS, as well as the CEA, regularly engage their respective communities of gatekeepers as well.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But I think the point that the Member is also trying to make, Sir, if I may, is that the key is in sensemaking.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is not just a question of imposing reporting requirements for the sake of the reporting requirements.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We would have to try and connect the dots.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Otherwise, it is just lots of signals and a lot of noise, which you cannot really do very much about.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: You have heard me talk about how the STRO had put in place a new data analytics system since February last year.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Minister of State Alvin Tan also talked about using COSMIC as a way of helping financial institutions make better sense of what information has already been captured through the STRs.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I should also say that each time we have a big bust like that, it also offers us fresh insights as to what kinds of signals we should be paying greater attention to.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The truth is that with even the best technology today, it is impossible to completely weed out money laundering.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: As the Minister put it so eloquently, it is not like looking for one needle in one haystack, but looking for one needle in multiple haystacks.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: And we also have to keep in mind that while good guys are getting smarter, perhaps the not-so-good guys are getting smarter even faster.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Having spent many years as the Asia Chief Executive Officer for a large Australian bank, I have lived through this experience myself –

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Parekh, can you get to your clarification, please?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: My question is: from most gatekeepers, intermediaries wish to enforce the anti-money laundering rules on a regular basis but often are not equipped or knowledgeable enough to ask the right questions during the process.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: So, perhaps the focus should be more on providing additional training and guidance for these intermediaries as well as potential gatekeepers to make sure that the right questions are asked.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Clearly, these indicators can be improved and we will continue to do so over time.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is certainly something that we will continue to uplift our capabilities in, and I am sure that Minister Indranee and her IMC will look into.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I think it is, in fact, the fourth of her terms of reference, if I heard her correctly.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For Minister Josephine, can I ask, based on the investigations so far, how was the $2.8 billion of funds placed in our system?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, how much was through our banking system and how much was through cash and then how much through other channels?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For Minister Indranee, may I ask, just now she answered the question on the cash transactions, although she said it is not appropriate to impose a quantum on the amount of cash to be used in transactions but I used to run a stockbroking company in Singapore, I can declare, and we report suspicious transactions as well.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I have shared with Members the extent to which I am able to reveal.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, as to his specific question, this is a level of detail that will have to be made known at a later stage.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I am not able to comment more on the details of this case – Mr Leong asked how they came to be placed in our financial system.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is a level of detail that we are not at liberty to discuss right now.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As you can well imagine, we are continuing to uncover new assets.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And if we are in the process of still trying to uncover the assets that have been procured as a result of these likely criminal proceeds, it would not be in the interest to say more at this point in time how the tracks were eventually identified.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I am also not sure that the question that the Member posed to Minister Indranee ought to be answered by her.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Or I am not sure that there was another level of detail that that he was seeking.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Can I clarify for the Minister that I am asking for specific amount of cash reported by the IRs, reported by the banks and reported by the property companies in the STR system?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Minister Indranee, is there anything that you like to add?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The first is, considering Singapore's amplified efforts to combat money laundering, would we be maintaining a universally welcoming stance for businesses or transition to a more discerning and selective methodology?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Are there plans to recalibrate our focus towards specific countries or demographic sectors?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The second is, as the Government introduced new protocols which are crucial to uphold our reputation as a reliable financial centre, these compliance measures would also require capacity development, skilled enhancement and adaptation periods for both frontline and backend personnel across all participating entities.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: How are we planning to bolster these capabilities without compromising the system's overall efficiency?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I think within his question is the concern that we will have knee-jerk reactions and overdo the reporting requirements as well as the other anti-money laundering obligations that we impose on different companies.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We always strive to be very calibrated in the statements of my colleagues and I; we were careful to emphasise that maintaining Singapore's overall friendliness towards legitimate businesses and legitimate investors.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: That must still be a priority for us to uphold.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is not a question of just layering on new measures without regard to their effectiveness but, really, weighing which are the new approaches or measures that will be necessary in order for us to uphold our reputation as a sound financial centre.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The second question is with regard to capability development and expanding the capacity of both our law enforcement agencies as well as our gatekeepers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is very much related to Mr Neil Parekh's points, and we totally agree with him and that is also an area of effort that we will have to step up.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I am sorry I was not sure that there was a third question specifically.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am mindful of the importance that the financial sector contributes to Singapore's GDP and, of course, our entrepot hub, trade hub as well.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, I just want to ask a supplementary question on the enhancement aspects of things, following this episode.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: First question I have for Minister of State Alvin is with regards to resources: how much we have spent on handling anti-money laundering in MAS to handle such things, including in terms of staffing, in terms of capacity building?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, it is somewhat related to the previous supplementary questions on staffing, resources.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Do we pale in comparison in terms of spending, in terms of spending, in term of staffing levels, going forwards as well?

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, we must make sure that our financial sector remains robust, both in terms of the vibrancy of the financial sector as well as being stringent to prevent illicit activities in the financial sector.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: In that case, in the second limb of that question, therefore, it is – how are we preparing our sector regulators, supervisors, for example, to be prepared and to be able to look out for these illicit activities?

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This department is responsible for three aspects, including regularly reviewing policies relating to money laundering and illicit financing, and also to then supervise how financial institutions manage these risks.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The third is also being forward looking and constantly looking at trends and typologies that will emerge, such as the typologies that have emerged in this case.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But we also know that there are some limitations.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We also understand that the volume – Minister Josephine Teo talks about 43,000 over 2020 to 2022, and 80% of these STRs are filed by financial institutions.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We will also share information with RTIG and other agencies, inter-Ministry agencies, to act on the typologies that I mentioned, that are emerging and quickly stop these illicit activities from gaining ground.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If I may, that may not be perhaps the way to look at how to strengthen effectiveness because it is not so much how much money you put into it but how effective you are and how much value you get for whatever money you put into it.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, we just take a broader look at the system.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There are so many parts of our system.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is not just who is staffing the STRO or who is staffing Police or who is staffing a particular Ministry.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Every bank officer who deals with people is a part of the system.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Every real estate agent is a part of the system.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And each of them has parts of the puzzle.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The real nature or the real key to uncovering the money laundering is making sense of the patterns because everybody owns a little piece of it.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: You file, you send it to STRO and I think Minister Josephine mentioned earlier, STRO is doing much more of the data analytics now.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, we will put in whatever resources are necessary to be able to make better sense of this and some of it will have to be done by technology, some of it has to be done through better training of whether it is real estate agents or anybody and the financial sector.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And then the real key is how do you design it in a way that pulls together all this information and a pattern emerges.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That is really how the detection and the capability building should be built up.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In the recent years, we have seen increased wealth influx into Singapore and some of these fund flows are now suspected to be part of the proceeds of criminal activities.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I am just wondering taken in total, what impact, implications or estimated effects will these developments and findings have on our economy – specifically financial, wealth management, asset management sectors – going forward?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The second one is for Minister Indranee, relating to the approvals granted to foreigners to buy landed properties in Singapore and, I think, it is well taken that the numbers have been very low.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: But just coming back to my PQ, I was just wondering about whether the Singapore Land Authority (SLA) specifically looks at money laundering, does some kind of money laundering checks as well when doing the assessments for these applications.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I think one of the criteria was also about exceptional economic contributions should be made to Singapore and I am just wondering about what sort of general factors are taken to account when making the assessment of whether or not these applications do meet these criteria.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: My third clarification is how many property agents, developers and owners have been investigated in the last three years for failing to exercise duties to conduct CDD/anti-money laundering-type checks and how are these investigations typically commenced?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Are they usually tip-offs or are they proactive investigations that are carried out to make sure that all these individuals and these professions are exercising their duties properly?

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I think the flow of funds speak to the robustness and the dynamism of Singapore's financial sector.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, we must and we will continue to build our financial sector, because it creates good jobs for Singaporeans and enhances our standing as an international financial centre.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: However, we know, given that there are millions of transactions every single day, that there will be some illicit funds.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But the majority of these transactions, as we had mentioned, are legitimate.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, it is very important that we do not throw the baby out with the bathwater.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The second part of this limb, as I had mentioned earlier on, is also the robustness of our AML/CFT regulations, that is really much in line with what international financial sectors have.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, it is strict enough, but we would also be very keen to make sure that, as both Mr Mark Lee as well as Mr Neil Parekh had mentioned, we remain open to global financial flows, investments, as well as talent.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Minister Indranee, I wanted to make the request to Ms He whether she would mind if her questions on real estate could be moved to when we cover the third segment?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I know it is sometimes not easy to frame it all together, but I can see that we are moving from the first segment to the second segment, which is on financial systems and sector.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, I will try to keep it in that way for all the questions, if possible.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I will come back to you, Ms He, when we come back to the real estate segment.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Alluding to Minister of State's earlier point about strengthening of MAS' capabilities and AMLD in respect of anti-money laundering, could the Minister of State share his perspective on how other international financial centres have dealt with financial institutions as well as complicit individuals who are implicated in money laundering cases?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: And then of course comparing this to Singapore's situation.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I think both Minister Teo and Minister Indranee had also mentioned this, and I thought it will be useful to also flesh this out.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Minister Teo mentioned, and I too have mentioned, that the very characteristics that make us a dynamic and open financial sector also makes it attractive to criminals.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But like other financial centres, Singapore is not unique to this challenge of money laundering.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: In Switzerland, for example, one individual was fined for failing to file an STR.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I have two supplementary questions for Minister of State Alvin Tan.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Does MAS have any roadmap to expand the COSMIC financial crime risks to new or known trends that may post a reputation risk?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: And how does MAS decide to disseminate such intelligence deriving from STRs in a timely manner to other financial institutions as part of the ACIP public-private partnership that have proven to be effective, especially when it is not uncommon that such money laundering suspects hop banks after their accounts were closed by the previous bankers?

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I think it is quite important just to understand whether if you open a bank account and you are affected, whether you can hop to another bank and whether the information will be shared.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: As the Member knows, MAS requires banks to abide by customer confidentiality provisions that is provided for in the Banking Act and this prohibits them from disclosing customer information.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: However, to prevent criminals from exploiting these weaknesses of each financial institution's understanding of their customers' risk profile is because that is limited by the information that the financial institution collects.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But in the interim, as we await the launch of COSMIC, MAS will monitor for material risk mitigation to financial institutions not yet on COSMIC, and then we will also take the preventive or supervisory measures to prevent or to mitigate such developments from taking place.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: In the meantime, also, banks can and should – and will be and are able to – alert other financial institutions of concerning trends, typologies and emerging risks through sharing information on our public-private platform, which Mr Don Wee mentioned, which is ACIP, so that mitigating factors and mitigating actions can be taken by financial institutions as well as Government agencies to thwart these efforts.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I have two clarifications for the Minister of State Mr Alvin Tan.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The	Minister of State has mentioned that one accused person involved in the money laundering incident has been linked to a tax-incentivised SFO, but upon application for that tax incentive, nothing suspicious had surfaced.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: So, I would like to clarify if the entity concerned is still enjoying the tax incentive that it has been granted, and if so, whether there are any plans underway to revoke the grant of that tax incentive?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I would also like to clarify that my original PQ related to the general grant of incentives to funds under sections 13D, 13O and 13U of the Income Tax Act and so not just incentives granted to SFOs.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: So, can the Minister of State confirm that within this wider scope of the question, that it is still the case that only one accused person has been linked to a tax-incentivised entity?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The first is, in cases where charities are found to be receiving donations by individuals that have been found guilty of money laundering, what are the recourse for charities if they have spent the said sums to serve the charities' beneficiaries, and if there will be any difference in recourse between charities who have filed STR compared to those who have not?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The second clarification is what are the duties of charity fundraising platforms – not just the charities, but the platforms – in protecting themselves against money laundering or terrorism financing abuse?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And thirdly, are there enhancements to the COC's controls and abilities to detect malicious actors from using charities for round tripping purposes?

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We will be covering these questions in the COC's advisory, which Minister Josephine Teo had mentioned.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: On the second question on the duties of charities and how to safeguard against money laundering and terrorist financing abuse, we expect charities to implement appropriate mitigating measures to safeguard themselves against potential abuse for illicit purposes, including money laundering and terrorist financing, as charities may be misused as conduits for the movement of illegal funds.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Charities should exercise vigilance in accepting donations, in particular, when the donors are unknown or unfamiliar to the charities, or when requests are made by donors to redirect part of the donations to unknown third parties for purposes that may be incongruent with the charities' charitable objectives.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: A charity should also perform reasonable due diligence checks on donors, so as to ascertain the legitimacy of the source of funds or donations received, especially when a substantial amount of donation is received from an unfamiliar or an unknown donor.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: If charities have reasonable grounds to suspect that any property may be connected to a criminal activity, as I mentioned earlier on, they are required to file an STR.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: On the third question, we will review if there are gaps found, and the COC has been engaging charities all of this while on AML/CFT measures, and we will continue these efforts.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We can only be as strong as our weakest link.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: In many jurisdictions, DNFBPs, such as lawyers, accountants and real estate agents are regulated in as much the same way as credit and financial institutions.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Actually, the report that Minister Josephine Teo quoted, the same FATF's report, went on to say, in Singapore, whilst it had good things to say, but it did go on to highlight Singapore's immature understanding of money laundering and terrorist financing risks amongst these players, the DNFBPs.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, I would like to ask the Minister for her assessment of what is the state of development in Singapore amongst the non-financial sector in combating money laundering and what more can we do to strengthen our system?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But this really could not be further from the reality because this case is a culmination of two years of painstaking planning.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Member was asking about my assessment of where we stand now.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I would say that, first and foremost, it is a strong and robust regime.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We could, for example, have just, at the beginning, taken out a few of the suspects, seized a few million dollars and called it a day.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We wanted to develop as full a picture as possible, go after the entire network.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Where there were suspicious indicators associated with any individual, we pursued it relentlessly.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And that is what the IMC will be looking at.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I am starting to go into the real estate segment, segment three.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I think my PQ was not fully answered.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: And I have some further clarifications for Second Minister Indranee.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, property agents tell me they often do not have many tools other than a Google search engine to conduct CDD.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: And I note that the Second Minister said the CEA is developing a one-stop webpage.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Minister Indranee, perhaps you could also address what Ms He Ting Ru raised just now on real estate.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Okay, perhaps I will take the question by Ms He Ting Ru first.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I think Ms He asked firstly, whether or not SLA carries out CDD.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The conveyancing lawyers, the lawyers and the financial institutions also do the checks.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, SLA is not the main interface with the people doing the purchases, and hence, they do not do anti-money laundering checks.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I think her second question was on the contributions for approvals.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As I mentioned earlier in my main answer when it comes to landed property, there are two approval regimes.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And the other is for land that was residential property that was developed specifically to market to an international clientele; and there is one – Sentosa Cove.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is the one in mainland Singapore, where the approval regime is stricter and, as I mentioned earlier, that is the one where we take into account, various things: the applicant must be a PR for at least five years and that is the one that requires the exceptional economic contribution to Singapore, that could include factors like, how much income taxes have been paid and what other contributions they have made.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For Sentosa Cove, which was developed specifically for an international clientele, generally speaking – if they are able to show identity and they are not allowed to own more than one landed property.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, should they not have any other residential property, approval is generally granted.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: [Please refer to "Clarification by Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development", Official Report, 3 October 2023, Vol 95, Issue 113, Correction By Written Statement section.] In my early answer, I said out of the 88 applications, only two were denied.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Ms He had asked in respect of the past five years, but the Estate Agents Act (EAA) and the regulations have been in place for only three years.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The EAA and regulations have been in place since 2021.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, that is the period you are referring to.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These agents failed to comply with regulations relating to obtaining, documenting and verifying the accuracy of identifying information of clients, and determining and documenting the risk assessment of clients engaging in money laundering or financing of terrorism.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: [Please refer to "Clarification by Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development", Official Report, 3 October 2023, Vol 95, Issue 113, Correction By Written Statement section.] So, basically fines and you can be suspended and have your licence revoked.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I think Mr Gerald Giam had asked about information sharing.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: With respect to COSMIC, that will have to be directed to Minister of State Alvin Tan.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But with respect to how we can better assist real estate agents, as I mentioned, CEA is looking at setting up the webpage to assist them.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We will step up on the training and on the guidelines.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Some other types of information they would have available to them are by way of ACRA searches, for example.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For higher risk transactions, they are required to do enhanced due diligence; they have to ask for information.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, if they are being represented by someone and the beneficial owner or the owner is not here, they would want to see, for example, a power of attorney and/or letter of authorisation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They might have to ask for sources of the income and the company's place of incorporation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The types of documentation differ, but essentially, CEA provides these guidelines and conducts trainings for the real estate agents, so that they will have a better idea of what to ask.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As part of the IMC that I will be chairing, we will look to see what more we can do to better equip real estate agents in this sector.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If a property seems like it is one of the more major vehicles for loopholes, potential loopholes in the money laundering process, I am wondering, at least for the IMC, will there be a disproportionate effort in better aligning anti-money laundering procedures for the real estate sector vis-à-vis other financial institutions?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I say this because many industry insiders share with us that they believe that there is at least a 10- to 15-year lag in terms of the quality of anti-money laundering regulations in the sector vis-à-vis the financial sector, more generally.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Indeed, we agree that more can be done.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We had already started to do more in this space which is why even before this case came about, we had already started to look at how we could strengthen the system.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Hence, the Real Estate Agents Act was passed in 2010 and came into effect in 2021, and the regulations that I mentioned as well.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We will certainly see what we can do to strengthen the regulations in this sector.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: [Please refer to "Clarification by Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development", Official Report, 3 October 2023, Vol 95, Issue 113, Correction By Written Statement section.]

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I have a clarification for the Minister of State Alvin Tan on the role of family offices.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I also want to take a step back to touch on Ms He Ting Ru's point about financial flows.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Family offices play an important role in our financial sector as well and I want to caution Members against seeing all SFOs in the same light as those that are charged or wanted.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Our regime is in line with international best practices, and so, these two prongs of making sure that we are dynamic and open, and that we also have strong robust controls, remain central to our functioning as a vibrant and trusted financial centre.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I am glad to hear that there are several levels of checks for real estate transactions to prevent money laundering.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Are the current checks sufficient and how do we ensure compliance for these checks?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For instance, how do we ensure that property agents are trained to their appropriate level to conduct anti-money laundering CDD?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Perhaps having some audit checks and also have them take compliance tests?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Given this case, would there be further measures to ensure that Singapore's property market is not being targeted or misused for money laundering activities beyond just filing STRs?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But I think that the key thing to remember is this: the obligation that they have is to file an STR.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, if something strikes them as suspicious, that is their main duty.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They do not have to carry out an entire investigation and crack the case themselves.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They do not have to do the job of CAD or SPF.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The key thing that the real estate agents and others in the non-financial sector have to do is to spot when something seems off, is inconsistent or cannot be explained.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Usually, when you are in the sector long enough, you get a sense and a feel of this, which is why these are the gatekeepers.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They are the ones who deal with these transactions constantly and after a while, you will be able to pick up when something is just not quite the way it ought to be.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, in response to the first question, the answer is there is always more that can be done and we will look at that as part of the IMC.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The other question that Mr Yip asked was what checks are in place to ensure that Singapore's property market is not being targeted or misused for money laundering activities.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: You can never ensure that we will not be targeted.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: You can never ensure 100% that it will not happen because, as much as we try to prevent, you can be sure of the fact that because of our status as a financial hub and financial centre, they would want to come here.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But you can make it a very inhospitable place if we can step up on prevention, detection and enforcement, which Minister Josephine Teo talked about.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The other thing which may not have registered on Members' consciousness is this – Minister Josephine Teo alluded to it – the monies that are being laundered, online gambling and other things, most of that took place outside of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: When they want to come here and use Singapore as a base for money laundering, most of them would try to keep their activities here clean.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, on the face of it, they would do their very best to be as legitimate as possible here because they want this to be the place where they flow the illicit money and it comes out clean.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Anybody who has watched "Breaking Bad" will know how this is done. "Better Call Saul" was an exposition on how you do money laundering.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In response to Mr Yip's question, when they come here, they are going to do their very best to look and feel and seem legitimate.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The illicit monies come from elsewhere and they would try to put it through legitimate transactions so that when they come out, they are clean.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I think I have addressed the Member's questions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If I have missed anything, perhaps Mr Yip would let me know.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is in relation to the purchase of landed properties in Sentosa by foreigners.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: If I recall correctly, I think the Minister mentioned that there were 88 transactions, of which two were not approved.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Just now, the Minister also responded in her response that SLA does not conduct commercial due diligence.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In this aspect, I just want to understand what the processes or checks that are in place by SLA when it comes to such approvals and what the circumstances behind the two that were not approved were and, given the context of what has happened in the last two months, whether there are plans to institute additional processes to make sure that there is an additional layer of defence on top of the work that CEA and agents are doing.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For the properties in Sentosa Cove, the foreigners who are non-PRs can acquire them and approvals are generally granted.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For example, if you own one Sentosa Cove property and you want to get another one, then because it is two properties, you may not get approval for that unless there is some good reason for it.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, the short answer is that the approvals are generally granted.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I do not have the details of the two that were rejected but I think the key message that I wanted to get across is that Sentosa Cove was developed with a specific marketing clientele in mind, which is an international clientele, which is the reason why approval is generally granted when they are purchased by foreigners.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I do not know the exact number but it is a much smaller proportion compared to the others.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I think Minister Josephine alluded to about 80% of the STRs as coming from the financial sector.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, for the real estate sector, it is a much smaller proportion.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: However, what I would like to emphasise is that the real estate agents are operating as part of an entire ecosystem, meaning that for any transaction of the property, there should be a bank involved – usually a financial institution; there should be a lawyer involved somewhere, the real estate agent or the property developer.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, because it is part of an ecosystem, just because a real estate agent may not have filed an STR may not in and of itself mean that anything suspicious may not be picked up.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: You have to see it in that broader picture.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But the percentage, compared to the others, is much lower.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I will be slowly moving on to the fourth segment concerning companies, immigration and work passes, just to let everyone know.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The first question is: how did the 10 offenders and their associates manage to buy so many properties?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Over a hundred properties were bought by them.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: How many of the associates were also involved?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The second question: while it is reported that there are more than 120 properties identified with the syndicate, why were there only 94 prohibition orders issued on the properties?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, I think that will make up the numbers that Mr Leong was asking about.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I think the newspaper reports had indicated that some of them were caught in Good Class Bungalows.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I think that may be what the Member is thinking about.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: My understanding is that those were rented properties, not purchased properties.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I do not think we can say they are offenders yet.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They may well be, but they are suspects at this stage.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Those details will have to come out later when the investigations are complete.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: She shared in her speech that there are frameworks to access work pass applications.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Quite a few of the suspects were clearly holding on to work passes and they were staying in very expensive places.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Furthermore, how does MOM intend to improve the way these checks are conducted, in light of the money laundering incident, to support the WOG effort?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: My third clarification is: if there were instances of these cases whereby the suspects were staying in places that were very expensive, were they surfaced and how were these addressed?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: MOM's work pass framework is intended to support Singapore in its economic growth.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It enables companies to bring in foreigners who are complementary to our local workforce, spurring new investments, new growth in areas like the digital economy and the green economy.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This will help us to transform our economy and also help us to seize new opportunities even amidst the uncertain global economic environment and geopolitical challenges in the medium term and we hope that this will ultimately create more good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: MOM conducts checks to ensure that our work pass framework is not circumvented.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In particular, we check whether there is false declaration of salaries and qualifications and whether companies have business operations to cover the declared salaries of these workers.
