speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As mentioned in the multiple Ministerial Statements made by my colleagues earlier, some individuals may abuse the work pass framework to enter Singapore to commit illicit activities, such as the present case of money laundering.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Some may pretend to be employed by companies that are actually inactive or dormant.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But others may operate companies with an active trading front to mask the movement of their ill-gotten gains.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Yet others still may own a portfolio of legitimate and illicit businesses.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Criminals will constantly find new ways to circumvent our laws and our regulations and update their methods over time, making the task of detection even more complex and more difficult.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: MOM's salary fraud checks should be, therefore, seen as a first layer of checks to detect companies that do not have business operations to cover the declared salaries of workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This first layer of checks is part of a larger WOG system of checks to safeguard against money laundering risks.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will need to continue to coordinate with the rest of Government to uncover increasingly complex money laundering operations.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: MOM uses data analytics to identify higher-risk work pass applications for greater scrutiny.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Where there is any sign of possible salary fraud, companies are required to show documentary proof of business operations and their abilities to pay salaries.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We may also carry out checks after the work passes have been issued.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Companies may be subject to further audits or asked for further proof after the work pass holder arrives in Singapore or, subsequently, at the point of renewal.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: MOM also responds to whistle-blower reports to investigate whether companies have ongoing business operations.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We continuously sharpen our checks to better identify such fraudulent applications.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For instance, we regularly update our data analytics with concluded fraud cases and enforcement findings, so that they can more accurately pinpoint and flag out applications that are potentially fraudulent.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We conduct audits to detect breaches and also to validate and strengthen our analytics.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Our enforcement teams are also trained to detect various forms of salary fraud.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In addition, as Minister Josephine Teo explained in her Ministerial Statement earlier, work pass applicants are screened against a database of blacklisted individuals.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: MOM will continue to sharpen our fraud checks based on real cases on the ground.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Learning from the profiles of companies and profiles of individuals involved in the money laundering incident, we will update our data analytics with high-risk archetypes and strengthen our checks on whether businesses are operational.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: However, I hope that all of us, Members in this House, appreciate and I want to emphasise this, that the majority of work pass holders come to Singapore to work and contribute to our economy.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We, therefore, must take a sensible approach to calibrating our checks so that we do not hurt bona fide employers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Second, on MOM's role in the WOG's efforts to manage money laundering risks and Mr Desmond Choo's question on how we will improve checks to better do so.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Across the Government, we will review how to tighten our verification checks at various points.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: MOM will be part of the committee and will support its efforts.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: With better sharing of information across agencies, MOM can improve our salary fraud checks and share salary fraud cases with other agencies to conduct further probes on whether the relevant individuals are also involved in illicit activities.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: MOM will continue to take enforcement action on work pass applicants, pass holders and companies who have been found to be involved in illicit activities.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Our work pass framework is part of a broader system that is working as a whole to prevent unscrupulous individuals from entering Singapore on the pretext of employment, though we can and we will review how to tighten our checks at various points.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: However, we will need to take a balanced approach in reviewing our checks.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Singapore is known to companies as a welcoming place to do business in, and access to both local and global talent is an important factor that they consider.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, I would like to ask the Minister of State or Minister Tan See Leng what is the Government's take on this, being tagged as a place for "Singapore-washing".

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: More importantly, how do we guard against companies with such intentions who could abuse their legal status as a Singapore-domiciled company to misrepresent themselves in other markets, for example, and which could do harm to our reputation or compromise on our position?

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I think we have reiterated these points throughout this afternoon and the points remain very clear.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: First, our success as an international and financial hub is premised on our status as a trusted and well-governed hub with a strong rule of law.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, the core response to the question is that Singapore will always remain attractive.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We hope that Singapore will continue to remain attractive.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But we must and we always must make sure that our AML/CFT standards are in place and prevention, detection and enforcements are in place at the same time, to keep Singapore open and connected and attractive to the flow of funds, to the flow of talent and to the flow of businesses.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I thought that since the Member has gotten MAS and MTI's perspective, perhaps I can share a little bit from MOM's perspective.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For our data analytics, we triangulate and work with various sector agencies, to drive and improve our data analytics.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The nature of data analytics is dependent on past cases that you can learn from and that is the learning model.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But it is important to note that, as a result of this particular incident, my sense is that it has strengthened us as a global hub.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Like what Minister Josephine Teo talked about, zero tolerance does not mean zero occurrence.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But the very fact that when this was surfaced, there was a WOG approach, carefully coordinated, very targeted, to eventually catch such a big web sends a very strong signal to the world that we continue to welcome global talent, we continue to welcome top-notch enterprises to come to set up, as long as you do your business honestly, earnestly and diligently.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I thought I would just like to briefly respond to the point that was raised by Member Mr Liang Eng Hwa.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For anyone to see value in being Singapore-washed, you must have something within Singapore that has attracted this way of thinking.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: You must be thought of as a jurisdiction of repute.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Your anti-money laundering regime must be held in high regard because, if it was not, why would it be useful to be Singapore-washed?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Having said that, it does not mean that we adopt a very lax attitude towards anyone who sees a benefit of Singapore-washing.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In fact, the more this is valuable to the bad actors, to the money launderers, the more we must be resolved to weed them out in order to uphold this standing.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, on the one hand, it is kind of worrying that money launderers, criminal actors, would want to think of using Singapore as a haven to create the impression of legitimacy.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But on the other hand, it must say something about the quality of our regime, too.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Either we opt out of it and say that this is all too high risk, we do not want to be in this field, we would rather stay out of it completely.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Or we say that we take the risks that come with it, we strengthen not just our preventive measures, but also our ability to detect and to take the criminals to task, the enforcement aspect of it, our capabilities and our consistency in approaching all of these issues as they come about.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I think we have to look at it overall, in terms of the benefits and the cost.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And overall, if we consider how it has enabled Singapore businesses to be held in very high regard wherever it is that they go in the world and if we also think about the benefits it brings to Singaporeans, in terms of the quality of jobs that we are able to provide, it is really incumbent upon us to make sure that our regime remains robust.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And that is what this whole exercise is about for setting up the IMC.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I take it that those are the only fines imposed so far.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Second question: with regard to the introduction of the COSMIC system, why should there be a problem with client confidentiality when the banks already share clients' credit data on the Credit Bureau?

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The first one is related to the Wirecard case, where only at $3.8 million was levied.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: That shows that when we first prevent and then we detect, we quickly enforce.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: That is the hallmark of our AML/CFT regime which, again, I had mentioned, is on par with international standards as defined also by FATF's assessment.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The licence of one of the financial institutions was revoked.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, it is not just financial penalties, but also other forms of penalties to deter, thwart and punish in that regard.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The composition fines were imposed on 14 financial institutions and reprimands were issued to two financial institutions.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Enforcement actions were also taken against 11 individuals.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, what I am trying to say is that, again, the third prong, the way that we enforce, is not just fines but there are also prohibition orders, reprimands and so on, so forth.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, it is a whole suite of it.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Again, if you tie that with the overall AML/CFT framework, it is in line with international jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Can I just ask Mr Leong to just repeat his question with regard to COSMIC, please?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: What I mean is that the banks currently already share client credit information on the Credit Bureau.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, that is already sharing of client's information.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, what is the problem of introducing COSMIC to share information that may be related to the money laundering activities?

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Just to clarify that credit information is very different from STRs.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I think Mr Leong would also appreciate that the direct sharing of financial institution's information to financial institution, on STR, for example, will need to be very carefully circumscribed.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: When I talked about this in May earlier on, Members who had spoken about the Financial Institutions (Miscellaneous Amendments) Bill that this House passed in May, had also expressed concerns about customer confidentiality.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, it cannot be that just because there is an urgent need, we move at a quick pace, at too fast a pace that we forget the concerns about customer confidentiality.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Again, I want to reiterate that financial institutions do not share STRs which only cover customer information.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: While the Minister of State is taking questions about COSMIC and we seem to be winding into this last segment of additional questions, if I could quickly follow up and ask a question that my hon friend Mr Gerald Giam had also posed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: What inhibitions currently exist that would preclude real estate agencies and other non-financial institutions facing money laundering pressure, from getting onto a platform such as COSMIC?

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I had wanted to respond to Member Gerald Giam's question earlier on, so this gives me an opportunity to do so.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We were talking about how COSMIC initially in the earlier stages by the six banks, is sharing information amongst one another.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This will include information from COSMIC when it is rolled out.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And where relevant, STRO, which is effectively Singapore's financial intelligence unit, may also share information and obtain this from COSMIC with law enforcement agencies to facilitate investigations and supervision.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Can I clarify that the Minister of State is of the opinion that our current regime, at the moment, we have only imposed $3.8 million fine on the banks, compared to the $1.45 billion deposits that are already in the system, is according to international standard?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The $3.8 million fine was issued in relation to one case – Wirecard.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Minister of State Alvin Tan had already pointed that out.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I am just reiterating what he has just said.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Member is asking at the moment what is the total number of fines levied on banks.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I believe we do not have the information right now.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If that is something that the Member is seeking, perhaps, I can advise him to file a PQ and then we can answer that specifically.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The point that the Member is trying to link together – this $1.45 billion – the case is still live.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is for the Courts subsequently to determine what should be done with them.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And, in any case, I do not think it is right to link the amount seized with the fines that are imposed on the bank, on completely unrelated things.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: There will have to be a proper investigation as to whether there were actors in the financial sector that contributed to this web that we have uncovered.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But until that has been properly settled, it is premature for you to draw any conclusions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I have two clarifications for the Second Minister for Home Affairs.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The first actually relates to something she said in her main speech about the red flags that alerted the authorities to this billion-dollar money laundering bust, if I can say it that way.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: She said that, in 2021, there were a few STRs filed by financial institutions and also by other companies.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, could she let us know which industries these other companies came from?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Were there property agencies, were there law firms, for example?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, that is my first question to clarify where these other companies came from, that filed the STRs related to this case?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The second clarification is this: several of the persons arrested and charged were reportedly wanted by Police authorities in China and it was in relation, I think, to possible organised crime activities by these people wanted by police in China.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, my question is, have the Chinese authorities been assisting us in our investigation in Singapore?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: And related to that, has there been any indication that any Chinese parties will be making a claim on any of the assets or funds that have been seized in Singapore?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As to whether we connect the dots only using STRs, the answer is no.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: There will also be suspicious transactions exchange of information with foreign counterparts.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I cannot comment specifically to what it is in this case; it is premature for me to reveal more but it would not be unusual.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Keep in mind also that there will be other sources of intelligence.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Police interact with a wide surface and these can also help to form a picture as to what is going on.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Just to clarify again – I wonder if she could, I do not know whether there are any operational issues – but whether she could confirm, whether the Chinese police authorities are actually assisting us in our investigation; and, secondly, about whether there have been any indications so far on whether they are making a claim on the assets seized?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Suffice to say that there would be a variety.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This was explained by the Minister for Finance in response to the PQ I filed as striking a balance between regulatory compliance and ease of doing business.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: From an anti-money laundering perspective, it makes sense to directly subject such asset holding companies to such requirements instead of relying on intermediaries.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Second, Sir, may I ask the hon Second Minister for Finance whether the Government would be minded to consider providing a Minister with powers to prescribe, through subsidiary legislation businesses that should be subject to CDD requirements?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Prior to this Police operation, I suspect not many Members would even know the existence of Bearbrick dolls, much less the fact that these dolls were allegedly purchased for money laundering purposes.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Currently, the CDD requirements are done via specific pieces of legislation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In time to come, there could be other items which may be the money launderer's favourite.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Speed would be essential to ensure our system can react to such developments.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Hence giving our Minister the power to prescribe businesses that will have to conduct CDD may, therefore, help.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I think his question really was with respect to foreign companies which do not do anything other than own property, should we not bring them under the ACRA regime and make them disclose any beneficial ownership?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Companies Act and ACRA look at companies which carry on business in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If you have a foreign company that does not carry on any business and the only thing it does is just buys a property, then strictly speaking, it is not carrying on business, it is just owning a property.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And, therefore, it is not caught by the Companies Act regime for registration with ACRA.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In fact, such a foreign company does not even need to be registered in Singapore at all.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It just is the entity that owns a property.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That is the reason why we do not require it come under ACRA.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But that is not to say that there would be no requirement to find out beneficial ownership of that foreign company because when they are buying the property, the financial institutions, the real estate agents and the lawyers who act, would have to make those inquiries as part of their due diligence, and so they would have that information and the law enforcement agencies can, if necessary, ask these intermediaries for that beneficial ownership information.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That said, when we do our review as part of the IMC, we will look at all relevant areas and if anything needs to be finetuned or changed, we will look at it.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And I think his final question was – I was not quite sure I have understood the full import of it – if Mr Murali could just clarify that.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: It would be a bit faster than the current situation where you have specific legislation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: For example, precious stones and metal dealers, through legislation, they would now have to deal with CDD requirements.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Just so that we can, hopefully, be at least at pace with the criminals.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The IMC will consider that request as part of its review.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is certainly not the bank's profits that you should use to weigh against the responsibility that we hold them to.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This $1.45 billion has to be properly sorted out in terms of ownership.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They just happen to sit in the bank accounts.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, I hope that Members understand that these two numbers have no business being talked about together.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I hope that makes it clear, Mr Speaker.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: When you want to uphold zero tolerance in money laundering, of course, you have to suppress the profit motive of the people involved.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Although the $1.45 billion does not belong to the bank, but the fact is that $2.8 billion has been placed in our system and most of it is in the banking system.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And now, the Minister has given me the information that $1.45 billion is still in the banking system at the moment.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Maybe now, we have frozen the funds so the funds cannot be used by the banks anymore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But in the process of allowing these funds to come into our banking system, that is a huge amount of money the banks have made.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: If we do not take away that amount of money, that means if we impose a fine on them equivalent to the amount of money that they have made – maybe that is not in line with international standards, then we can adjust it a bit – but in terms of the amount of money that we are talking about in this case that has come into our banking system, do you know how much money the banks potentially have been making?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: You cannot say that these are two different issues.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: It reflects that the regulators do not appreciate that this is the way that the bank makes money, with this whole thing.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Nobody disputes that our financial institutions have a responsibility to uphold the strict measures that we will take against money launderers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Nobody is also saying that if they were to breach their obligations, they should not be taken to task.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In fact, what I have presented and what Minister of State Alvin Tan has presented point to the seriousness with which we hold the financial institutions to their obligations.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: What I seem to be hearing Mr Leong say is that, "Aha, you have found these amounts in your system.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And therefore, it must point to some action on the part of the financial institutions in facilitating this, in helping to make this happen".

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I am saying until we get to the bottom of things, this is not the right way to think about it.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The correct way to think about it is that the entire machinery that we have put in place was able to uncover such a web.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I mentioned this earlier in my Statement and the response to some questions that were posed by Members – would we be happier if we had acted at an earlier stage in the investigations and then uncovered a smaller web?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Or are we in the better position to have rooted out more of these activities?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We should continue to keep this number in perspective.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It speaks to the strength of our system to be able to uncover these suspected criminal proceeds.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: That is what we must continue to strengthen.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: That is what this effort is all about.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: There is a variety, there is a spectrum of it.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I think these are parameters we need to be aware of and these are parameters that the financial institutions know.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: As I mentioned in my Ministerial Statement earlier on, it is a priority for MAS.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong, if you have a new clarification, I will allow it, but I will not allow any repeat of the same clarifications you have asked.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: First of all, Speaker, Sir, I did not say that our banks have facilitated money laundering.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The Minister has said something that bordered on that implication.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: What I am saying is, with all the good intentions and measures that our banks have taken and MAS has asked our banks to take, we still landed with this case.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We have to demonstrate to our gatekeepers – most of our gatekeepers are the banks – that they must do their job properly.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: They must continue to do their job properly.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: In relation to the amount of money that has come into our system and the potential amount of profits that the banks can make from it, we must have penalties that are proportional to the potential profits that can be made if in the future, the verdict of the case has come out and it is demonstrated that some of the banks have been short on their anti-money laundering measures.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: What I take from the Minister today is that so far, only a few banks have —

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong, if you can get to your clarification, to the point.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Only a few banks, we are very sure that they are at fault.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But the other banks, we have to wait for the Court.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: That is what I get from the Minister.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Nothing that Minister of State Alvin Tan or I said implicate the banks right now.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We have only stated the facts about where the monies were found and how we seized them.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If that is his clarification, that he is not making a sweeping statement that our banks have been complicit, I think I welcome that clarification.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong, if you would like to clarify Minister's clarification to you.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: That is exactly what I was saying just now.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I did not say our banks are complicit in this scheme.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: What I am saying is how our rules will play out in ensuring our system continues to be robust and more robust in the future.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: What the Minister has said is that —
